title: Motion design and transitions
summary: Operational rules for purposeful motion, reduced motion, shared easing, compositor-friendly properties, focus during transitions, and autoplay loops. Each rule links the CSS or WCAG page for that subject.

rules.title: Motion explains change
rules.intent: Animate to show a change of state, a spatial relationship, or feedback, and treat everything else as removable
principles: Use a transition or animation when it shows where something went, what changed, or that an action registered
Motion that does not carry information is non-essential. WCAG 2.3.3 requires interaction-triggered motion animation to be disableable unless it is essential
Declarative transitions are easier to create, and easier for a user agent to slow or turn off. That is a reason to keep them few, not a reason to animate every update
antiPatterns: Animating every visible item on every rerender
acceptance: Each animation states what change it explains, or it is absent
limitations: CSS Snapshot 2026 lists Animations and Transitions as safe to release before Candidate Recommendation, and also groups them with modules of rough interoperability. Behavior in edge cases can still differ

rules.title: Respect reduced motion
rules.intent: When prefers-reduced-motion is reduce, non-essential motion does not run, and the task still works
principles: prefers-reduced-motion: reduce means the person asked the system to minimize non-essential motion
Ship the still presentation as the base, and add motion only inside prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference. Or turn the motion off inside reduce. Either way the reduced setting has a usable result
A change of color, blur, or opacity that does not change perceived size, shape, or position is not motion animation under WCAG 2.3.3
antiPatterns: Motion remains mandatory for sensitive users
acceptance: With the system set to reduce, interaction-triggered motion is off unless it is essential, and the action still completes
limitations: The media feature is in Media Queries Level 5. CSS Snapshot 2026 lists it as safe to release before Candidate Recommendation. C39 is a sufficient technique for 2.3.3, not the only one

rules.title: Reusable motion tokens
rules.intent: Share duration and easing with custom properties, using the easing functions CSS already defines
principles: Define repeated durations and easing curves once, as custom properties, and use those for the same kind of change
Use the easing functions in CSS Easing: linear, ease, ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out, cubic-bezier, or steps
A one-off timing on a single view needs a reason
acceptance: Repeated transitions read their duration and easing from a shared custom property
limitations: CSS defines the functions and the custom-property mechanism. It does not require a named token scale. The scale is a project decision

rules.title: Performant properties
rules.intent: Keep routine motion on transform and opacity so it does not force layout or paint every frame
principles: Move and scale with transform. Show and hide with opacity. Those stay on the compositor for routine transitions
Before animating any other property, check whether it triggers layout or paint. Avoid that unless the effect needs it
will-change is a hint for an element that is about to change, applied for that change and removed after. It is not a default on every node
antiPatterns: Animating large layout properties each frame
acceptance: Routine transitions use transform or opacity, and a layout-property animation has a stated reason
limitations: Transforms Level 1 is in the official CSS definition. will-change is grouped with rough interoperability. The compositor guidance is from web.dev, which is an authoring article, not the spec

rules.title: Animate entry and exit coherently
rules.intent: Let entry and exit finish without taking keyboard focus or blocking the rest of the page
principles: Entry and exit of the same component use the same easing family, so the motion reads as one system
An animation that starts from a user action can be turned off under prefers-reduced-motion unless it is essential
A moving layer must not hold focus in a way that makes the rest of the page unusable. Focus lands on the control that should have it when the transition ends
acceptance: Keyboard focus is correct when the transition ends, including when reduced motion is on
limitations: WCAG 2.2.2 says a pause control must not tie up focus. It does not require the exit to be shorter than the enter. A shorter exit is a project choice, not a spec rule

rules.title: Avoid distracting loops
rules.intent: Give a way to pause, stop, or hide motion that starts by itself, lasts more than five seconds, and sits beside other content
principles: Moving, blinking, or scrolling content that starts automatically, lasts more than five seconds, and is shown with other content needs a mechanism to pause, stop, or hide it
The mechanism must not trap the user. Stopping only while the animation has focus, then restarting when focus leaves, does not qualify
Hover, focus, or scrolling into view can count as an automatic start. Essential motion, where the motion is the activity, is the exception
In a task UI, do not run an ambient loop next to the primary action
antiPatterns: Pulsing graphics competing with primary form
acceptance: Any automatic loop longer than five seconds can be paused, stopped, or hidden without losing the task
limitations: The five-second threshold and the essential-activity exception are WCAG 2.2.2. A shorter decorative loop can still fail 2.3.3 when a user interaction starts it
